articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities in Counter Narcotics and Cyber-related Actions, Issues New General Licenses
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations today targeting entities involved in counter narcotics and cyber-related activities. This action aims to disrupt illicit networks that pose a threat to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued a new Illicit Drugs General License to facilitate certain humanitarian-related transactions. Additionally, an amended Russia-related General License was released, alongside updated Frequently Asked Questions, providing further guidance on permissible activities.

These measures underscore OFAC's ongoing commitment to combating illicit financial flows and adapting its sanctions programs to address evolving threats, while also ensuring that legitimate activities can continue.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today announced new designations under its counter terrorism authorities. These actions target individuals and entities identified as supporting terrorist organizations and their activities globally.

The designations aim to sever financial and material support networks, thereby limiting the ability of these groups to plan and execute attacks. This move is part of a broader strategy to combat global terrorism and protect U.S. national security interests.
Further details regarding the specific individuals and entities designated were made available on the Treasury Department's website.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Joint Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today announced a series of designations combining counter narcotics and counter terrorism authorities. This joint action targets illicit networks involved in both drug trafficking and the financing of terrorist activities.

These designations aim to disrupt the convergence of these criminal enterprises, which often rely on similar financial and logistical channels. By targeting both aspects simultaneously, OFAC seeks to enhance the effectiveness of its sanctions programs.
The Treasury Department emphasized its commitment to working with international partners to dismantle these dangerous networks and protect the global financial system from abuse.

articles.headline: OFAC Updates Iran Designation List
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an update to its Iran-related designations. This action reflects ongoing efforts to address the Iranian regime's destabilizing activities and its support for terrorism.

The specific details of the updated designations were published on the OFAC website, providing clarity for individuals and entities subject to U.S. sanctions. These updates are part of a continuous review and adjustment of sanctions programs to ensure their effectiveness.
The U.S. government reiterates its commitment to holding the Iranian regime accountable for its actions and preventing it from acquiring resources that could be used to further its malign agenda.

articles.headline: New Iran-related Designations Announced by OFAC
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today announced new Iran-related designations. These actions are part of the ongoing pressure campaign against the Iranian regime, targeting its various illicit activities.

The designations aim to further restrict the Iranian government's access to the international financial system and its ability to fund its nuclear program, ballistic missile development, and support for regional proxy groups.
OFAC continues to monitor and adapt its sanctions to counter the evolving threats posed by Iran, working to prevent the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction and promote regional stability.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities for Cyber-related and Transnational Criminal Activities, Issues Cuba-related Actions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today announced new designations targeting entities involved in cyber-related activities and transnational criminal organizations. These actions aim to disrupt malicious cyber actors and criminal networks that threaten U.S. national security and economic stability.

In addition to these designations, OFAC also issued new Cuba-related designations and published a Cuba-related determination. These measures reinforce the U.S. government's policy towards Cuba, addressing concerns related to human rights and support for other authoritarian regimes.
The Treasury Department continues to leverage its sanctions authorities to combat a wide range of illicit activities, protecting the integrity of the global financial system.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements New Iran-related Designations and Amends Venezuela-related General License
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today announced new Iran-related designations and provided updates to certain Iran-related listings. These actions are part of the ongoing effort to counter the Iranian regime's destabilizing behavior.

In conjunction with these measures, OFAC published an Iran-related OFAC Alert to inform the public about potential risks and illicit schemes. Additionally, an amended Venezuela-related General License was issued, along with a new Frequently Asked Question, offering updated guidance on permissible transactions.

These comprehensive actions demonstrate OFAC's commitment to maintaining pressure on both the Iranian and Venezuelan regimes while providing necessary clarity for legitimate humanitarian and other authorized activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today issued an amended Iran-related General License. This amendment aims to clarify and adjust certain authorizations related to transactions involving Iran.

General Licenses are often issued to ensure that sanctions do not unduly impact humanitarian aid, personal remittances, or other specific categories of transactions. The details of this amended license are available on the OFAC website.
This action reflects OFAC's ongoing process of reviewing and refining its sanctions programs to maximize their effectiveness while minimizing unintended consequences.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities in North Korea and Democratic Republic of the Congo
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today announced new designations targeting entities in North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). These actions are part of broader efforts to address threats to international peace and security.

The North Korea designations aim to counter the regime's weapons of mass destruction programs and its illicit revenue generation activities. The DRC-related designations target individuals and entities involved in human rights abuses and corruption, which fuel conflict and instability in the region.
These measures underscore the U.S. commitment to promoting accountability and upholding international norms against proliferation, human rights violations, and corruption.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Reaches Settlement Agreement with OFAC
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc. today. The settlement resolves alleged violations of OFAC sanctions regulations.

Details of the settlement, including the specific nature of the violations and the agreed-upon penalty, were made public on the OFAC website. Such agreements often involve companies taking remedial measures to improve their compliance programs.
This action highlights OFAC's continued enforcement efforts to ensure that U.S. companies adhere to sanctions requirements and maintain robust compliance frameworks.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Fined Over $1.5 Million by OFAC
body: Extreme Networks, Inc. has agreed to pay $1,529,685 to settle its potential civil liability for apparent violations of sanctions programs administered by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC).

The settlement underscores OFAC's commitment to enforcing U.S. sanctions laws and holding companies accountable for compliance failures. The specific details of the violations were outlined in the settlement agreement.
This penalty serves as a reminder to all companies of the importance of robust sanctions compliance programs to prevent unauthorized transactions with sanctioned entities or regions.

articles.headline: Bank of America, N.A. Assessed Over $11 Million Civil Penalty by OFAC
body: Bank of America, N.A. has been assessed a civil penalty of $11,662,930 by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for apparent violations of sanctions regulations.

This significant penalty highlights the critical need for financial institutions to maintain comprehensive and effective sanctions compliance programs. The violations involved transactions that contravened U.S. foreign policy objectives.
OFAC continues to prioritize enforcement actions against financial institutions that fail to prevent illicit financial flows and ensure adherence to sanctions requirements.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Fined Over $175,000 by OFAC
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics has agreed to pay $175,015 to settle its potential civil liability for apparent violations of sanctions programs administered by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC).

The settlement underscores the importance of due diligence and compliance for logistics and shipping companies in preventing the movement of goods to or from sanctioned jurisdictions or entities. The specific nature of the violations was detailed in the settlement agreement.
OFAC's enforcement action serves as a reminder that all parties involved in international trade must ensure their operations comply with U.S. sanctions regulations.

articles.headline: Individual Assessed Over $1.4 Million Civil Penalty by OFAC

This action highlights that OFAC's enforcement extends to individuals as well as corporate entities, emphasizing personal responsibility for adherence to sanctions laws. The details of the violations were made public in the settlement document.
OFAC continues to pursue enforcement actions to deter illicit activities and ensure compliance across all sectors and individuals subject to U.S. jurisdiction.

articles.headline: Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors
body: In this interim final rule (IFR), the Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. First, this rule establishes new restrictions which will apply for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models. Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in Country Group D:5 or Macau, as part of complying with this new control. The license requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat. Second, in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs)--countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The license requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met. Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR and will consider a range of consequences for such countries, such as import restrictions, new license requirements on advanced semiconductor exports, downgrading the country's status in the U.S. export control regime, and Entity List designations and temporary export prohibitions for foreign persons involved in such activities. Third, this IFR amends the presumptions which front-end chips fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips. These amendments reduce the number of pathways to overcome the presumptions for chip designers located in destinations which face a license requirement for SI chips. This change gives the U.S. government critical oversight over companies headquartered in certain countries that seek to leverage advanced semiconductor production capabilities in third countries. Finally, the IFR formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The AI Diffusion Rule has never been enforced. The regulatory changes in this rule formalize the rescission of the AI Diffusion Rule, which the Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced in May 2025.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
